# Agent Guide to pnpm Repository

This document provides context and instructions for AI agents working on the pnpm codebase.

The repository contains three products:

- The **TypeScript pnpm v11 CLI** — `pnpm11/`.
- The **Rust pnpm v12 CLI (pacquet)** — `pnpm/`. pnpm v12 is the target for new feature development. See [`pnpm/AGENTS.md`](./pnpm/AGENTS.md) for pacquet-specific rules; it adds to (and never contradicts) the conventions below.
- The **Rust pnpr registry server** — `pnpr/`. See [`pnpr/AGENTS.md`](./pnpr/AGENTS.md) for pnpr-specific rules; it adds to (and never contradicts) the conventions below.

Sections below marked "(TypeScript only)" apply to TypeScript code only; they do not apply to Rust code in `pnpm/` or `pnpr/`. Everything else applies repo-wide unless a nested `AGENTS.md` specializes it.

## Project philosophy

Apply [PHILOSOPHY.md](./PHILOSOPHY.md) when implementing, triaging, or reviewing
changes. It defines the core requirements and the approach to existing
capabilities, abstractions, compatibility, and releases.

## pnpm v12 and v11 development policy

pnpm v12, implemented in Rust under `pnpm/`, is the target for new development. pnpm v11, implemented in TypeScript under `pnpm11/`, is maintained for bug fixes.

**Implement new features only in pnpm v12. Do not add them to pnpm v11.** A feature that intentionally exists only in v12 is not a parity gap.

For bug fixes, first determine which versions contain the bug. If the bug is present in both v11 and v12, implement and test the fix in both stacks. Keep their observable behavior aligned for the affected functionality, including command-line flags and defaults, environment-variable handling, lockfile/manifest/state-file formats, error codes and messages, log emissions parsed by `@pnpm/cli.default-reporter`, store layout, and hook semantics. If the bug exists in only one version, fix only that version.

When a shared bug fix cannot be completed in both stacks in the same PR, call out the missing implementation in the PR description so it can be added before the PR lands.

The pacquet-side version policy is in [`pnpm/AGENTS.md`](./pnpm/AGENTS.md#version-policy).

## Website documentation

User documentation lives in `pnpm/docs/` for v12, `pnpm11/docs/` for v11,
and `pnpr/docs/` for the registry. Update
the affected version's docs and sidebar in the same PR as a behavior change.
See [DOCUMENTATION.md](./DOCUMENTATION.md) for local previews and release publishing.
The blog and website application remain in pnpm/pnpm.io.

## Repository Structure

The pnpm codebase is a monorepo managed by pnpm itself. The root contains functional directories organized by domain:

### TypeScript pnpm v11 Core Directories

-   `pnpm11/pnpm/`: The CLI entry point and main package.
-   `pnpm11/pkg-manager/`: Core package management logic (installation, linking, etc.).
-   `pnpm11/resolving/`: Dependency resolution logic (resolvers for npm, tarballs, git, etc.).
-   `pnpm11/fetching/`: Package fetching logic.
-   `pnpm11/store/`: Store management logic (content-addressable storage).
-   `pnpm11/lockfile/`: Lockfile handling, parsing, and utilities.

### CLI & Configuration

-   `pnpm11/cli/`: CLI command implementations and infrastructure.
-   `pnpm11/config/`: Configuration management and parsing.
-   `pnpm11/hooks/`: pnpm hooks (readPackage, etc.).
-   `pnpm11/cli/commands/src/completion/`: Shell completion support.

### Other Functional Directories

-   `pnpm11/network/`: Network-related utilities (proxy, fetch, auth).
-   `pnpm11/workspace/`: Workspace-related utilities.
-   `pnpm11/exec/`: Execution-related commands (run, exec, dlx).
-   `pnpm11/engine/runtime/commands/`: Node.js environment management.
-   `pnpm11/cache/`: Cache-related commands and utilities.
-   `pnpm11/patching/`: Package patching functionality.
-   `pnpm11/releasing/`: Release and publishing utilities.

### Shared Utilities

-   `pnpm11/fs/`: Filesystem utilities.
-   `pnpm11/crypto/`: Cryptographic utilities.
-   `pnpm11/text/`: Text processing utilities.

### Rust Projects

-   `pnpm/`: The Rust pnpm v12 CLI. Self-contained sub-project with its own crates, tests, and tooling — see [`pnpm/AGENTS.md`](./pnpm/AGENTS.md).
-   `pnpr/`: The pnpm-compatible npm registry server. Self-contained sub-project with its own crates, tests, and tooling — see [`pnpr/AGENTS.md`](./pnpr/AGENTS.md).

## Setup & Build (TypeScript only)

To set up the environment and build the project:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm run compile
```

To compile a specific package:

```bash
pnpm --filter <package_name> run compile
```

**Important:** The TypeScript pnpm v11 CLI e2e tests (in `pnpm11/pnpm/test/`) use the **bundled** `pnpm11/pnpm/dist/pnpm.mjs`, not the individual package `lib/` outputs. After changing any TypeScript package, you must rebuild the bundle before running e2e tests:

```bash
pnpm --filter pnpm run compile
```

This runs `tsgo --build`, linting, and `pnpm run bundle` (which bundles all TypeScript packages into `pnpm11/pnpm/dist/pnpm.mjs`). Without this step, e2e tests will use a stale bundle and your changes won't be tested.

## Testing

Run the selection that covers what you changed, not the whole repository: the
full suite takes a lot of time. This applies to every product here, TypeScript
and Rust alike. Let CI run the rest — it runs the full Rust suite on
Linux, macOS, and Windows and the full TypeScript suite for every pull request.
The [`testing-changes`](./.agents/skills/testing-changes/SKILL.md) skill covers
how to derive that selection from the diff in each product, and
[`pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md`](./pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md#automated-checks) has the Rust
workspace's checks, including the one case that does call for a full local run:
a change whose affected set cannot be named, such as the workspace manifest,
the lockfile, or the toolchain.

The rest of this section is TypeScript only.

Run tests for a specific project instead:

```bash
# From the project directory
pnpm test

# From the root, filtering by package name
pnpm --filter <package_name> test
```

Or better yet, run tests for a specific file:

```bash
pnpm --filter <package_name> test <file_path>
```

Or a specific test case in a specific file:

```bash
pnpm --filter <package_name> test <file_path> -t <test_name_pattern>
```

## Linting (TypeScript only)

To run all linting checks:

```bash
pnpm run lint
```

## Never ignore test failures

Do not dismiss a failing test as a "pre-existing" failure that is unrelated to your changes. Every test failure must be investigated and fixed. If a test was already broken before your changes, fix it as part of your work — do not silently skip it or treat it as acceptable.

## Setting Up the Environment

The repository holds two implementations of the same package manager: the TypeScript pnpm CLI and the Rust `pacquet` port (plus the Rust `pnpr` registry server). Most contributions touch Rust, but the two stacks share one workspace, so set up both.

### JavaScript and TypeScript CLI

1. Install pnpm using one of the [official installation methods](https://pnpm.io/installation). **Do not use Corepack.** The scripts in this repository invoke pnpm through the `pn` and `pnx` aliases, which the official installation methods create. Corepack only provides the `pnpm` and `pnpx` commands, so with a Corepack-managed pnpm the build fails with errors like `pn: Permission denied` ([pnpm/pnpm#12448](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/12448)).
1. Set up the Rust toolchain first, as described under [Rust toolchain and git hooks](#rust-toolchain-and-git-hooks). `pnpm install` also installs the Rust dependencies and runs `cargo`, so it fails when `cargo` is not on `PATH`.
1. Run `pnpm install` in the root of the repository to install all dependencies.
1. Run `pnpm add ./pnpm11/pnpm/dev -g` to make pnpm from the repository available in the command line via the `pd` command.
1. Run `pnpm run compile` to create an initial build of pnpm from the source in the repository.
1. Now you can change any source code file and run `pd [command] [flags]` to run `pnpm` directly from the source code by compiling all the files without typechecking in memory.
1. Alternatively, for recompiling all the projects with typechecking after your changes, again run `pnpm run compile` in the root of the repository.
1. Run the tests for what you changed rather than the whole repository, which takes a long time: `pnpm test` inside a project's directory, `pnpm --filter <project name> test` from the root, or `pnpm --filter <project name> test <file path>` for a single file. `pnpm run test-all` runs the whole TypeScript suite on the rare occasion you need it; the Rust and `pnpr` suites are separate, and are covered in [`pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md`](./pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md).

Some of the e2e tests run node-gyp, so you might need to install some build-essentials on your system for those tests to pass. On Fedora, install these:

```shell
sudo dnf install make automake gcc gcc-c++ kernel-devel
```

### Rust toolchain and git hooks

Rust is now the primary language in this repository, so most contributions need a working Rust toolchain and the Rust developer tools. The Rust workspace (`Cargo.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, `justfile`) lives at the repository root; run `cargo` and `just` from there.

1. Install [`rustup`](https://rustup.rs). You do not need to select a toolchain by hand. `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version the project builds with, and `rustup` installs it, together with `clippy` from the pinned `default` profile, the first time you run `cargo` inside the repository.

2. Install [`just`](https://just.systems) (the task runner) and [`cargo-binstall`](https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall), then install the task tools from the repository root:

   ```shell
   just init
   ```

   `just init` installs `cargo-nextest`, `cargo-watch`, `cargo-insta`, `typos-cli`, `taplo-cli`, `wasm-pack`, and `cargo-llvm-cov` (via `cargo binstall`), plus `cargo-fixit` (pinned to `0.1.15` via `cargo install cargo-fixit@0.1.15 --locked`, since `cargo-fixit` has no prebuilt binaries). `cargo-fixit` backs the `just fix` task. It also builds the pinned pnpm rustfmt fork described below.

   Because `cargo-fixit` is built from source, it needs a complete OpenSSL development installation — headers and libraries — which its `openssl-sys` dependency looks for at build time. Without one, `just init` fails while installing `cargo-fixit`, before it reaches the rustfmt step, with `failed to run custom build command for openssl-sys`. Install it first: `sudo dnf install openssl-devel` on Fedora, `sudo apt install libssl-dev pkg-config` on Debian and Ubuntu. If OpenSSL is installed somewhere `openssl-sys` does not look — under a Homebrew prefix, for instance — point it at that existing installation with `OPENSSL_DIR`, for example `export OPENSSL_DIR=$(brew --prefix openssl@3)`. Note that `OPENSSL_DIR` only locates an installation; it is not a substitute for one.

3. Install the dylint tools, which `just init` does not cover, **from source**:

   ```shell
   cargo install cargo-dylint dylint-link
   ```

   Install these from source rather than with `cargo binstall`. The prebuilt `cargo-dylint` binaries reference the `dylint_driver` crate at the path where they were built, so building the per-toolchain driver fails locally with an error that points at a nonexistent `.../dylint/driver` directory. A `cargo install` build resolves the driver against your local cargo registry and works.

`pnpm install` at the repository root installs the Rust dependencies alongside the JavaScript ones. It reads `Cargo.lock`, links the registry crates into `.pnpm/crates/crates-io` and the git-sourced ones into `.pnpm/crates/git`, and points Cargo at both through the source replacement block committed in `.cargo/config.toml`. `cargo build` and `cargo test` work as before, and `cargo metadata --locked --offline` confirms that every dependency resolves without network access.

Every crate reaches the build this way, in CI as well as locally. Cargo resolves nothing from its own registry, so a cargo command needs an install behind it. Run `pnpm install` after a fresh clone, and again after any checkout that moves `Cargo.lock`, a `git bisect` step included. Until you do, `cargo build` fails with `failed to load source for dependency`. Add crates with `pnpm add`: `cargo add` resolves against the replaced source and cannot find a crate that is not already installed.

The block is a function of `Cargo.lock`, so an install regenerates it byte for byte and leaves `git status` clean. It changes only when a git-sourced dependency moves to a new revision, and that change belongs in the same commit as the lockfile. Rust CI fails if the two drift apart.

Make sure `~/.cargo/bin` is on your `PATH`, ahead of any system-wide Rust in `/usr/bin`. `rustup`'s installer adds this entry through `~/.cargo/env`; ensure your shell sources it. This matters for the git hooks. The `pnpm install` step above wires up husky. Its `pre-commit` hook formats the Rust files being committed, as described under [Rust formatting](#rust-formatting), and its `pre-push` hook runs the Rust checks in `pnpm/scripts/pre-push-rust.sh` (format, doc, dylint, typos) alongside the TypeScript compile and lint. That script locates `cargo`, `rustup`, `taplo`, `typos`, and `cargo-dylint` through `PATH`, and it **skips** a check when the tool is not found rather than failing. A push that appears to pass locally with the tools off `PATH` has silently skipped the format, doc, and dylint checks, so those problems surface only in CI.

For the full Rust development workflow (checks, tests, benchmarks, and the code style guide), see [`pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md`](./pnpm/CONTRIBUTING.md).

```shell
node pnpm/scripts/rustfmt.mjs --all
node pnpm/scripts/rustfmt.mjs --all -- --check
```

report.overview: At commit b2ef6cb63b8b7cb93d6b57f0d2efedf25d7c1385, this repository contains the Rust pnpm v12 CLI, the maintained TypeScript pnpm v11 CLI, and pnpr, a Rust registry server. It serves developers managing dependencies, workspaces, scripts, and releases, plus operators hosting or proxying packages. Distinctive mechanisms include content-addressed installation, separate wanted and installed lockfile state, policy verification, JavaScript hooks, and an optional server-assisted resolution path. This brief reflects bounded source inspection, including three concrete flows; it is not exhaustive coverage or runtime validation.
report.agent_prompt:
Investigate pnpm from the checked-out revision before making changes. This brief was grounded in commit b2ef6cb63b8b7cb93d6b57f0d2efedf25d7c1385; verify drift if HEAD differs. The repository contains three products: Rust pnpm v12 under pnpm/, TypeScript pnpm v11 under pnpm11/, and the Rust pnpr registry server under pnpr/. New CLI features belong in v12. For bugs, establish which supported implementations are affected and preserve observable agreement when fixing both. pnpr is a sibling server with its own behavior and configuration contracts.

Read AGENTS.md, PHILOSOPHY.md, the owning product's AGENTS.md, and its contribution guide. Search for existing capabilities before adding helpers or dependencies. The Rust products share the root Cargo workspace. Root package.json and pnpm-workspace.yaml define development scripts, pipelines, and concurrency groups. Prefer those scripts for authorized execution. Dependency setup is unusual: pnpm installs Cargo dependencies into replacement sources, so a fresh checkout or changed Cargo.lock can require setup before Cargo commands work.

For CLI startup, begin with pnpm/crates/cli/src/bin/main.rs and src/lib.rs. Raw shim dispatch precedes argument rewriting. Pinned-package-manager dispatch, completion, and an up-to-date install shortcut may finish before normal command execution. Commands are registered in cli_args/cli_command/commands.rs. Configuration, State, reporters, and command routing are separate responsibilities.

For installation, follow cli_args/install.rs into State::install, package-manager/src/install/entry_points.rs, install/run.rs, and install/run/execution.rs. Identify the local versus pnpr branch, frozen versus fresh branch, selected workspace scope, and lockfile-only or dry-run conditions. Read dispatch.rs before changing freshness decisions. Follow materialization into apply_materialization.rs and its commit module. Preserve the sequence that writes module metadata and the current lockfile before publishing workspace freshness. Treat verification gates, lifecycle execution, filtered metadata, and store-index teardown as contracts.

For pnpr, start with main.rs, server.rs, and server/routing.rs. Production startup loads persistent authentication and performs registry journal recovery before accepting connections. The router convenience API uses in-memory auth. Package reads resolve a declared registry source and enforce access before serving data. Upstream metadata caching and tarball caching have different freshness rules. New tarballs bind to declared integrity before cache promotion; warm cache behavior depends on whether OSV screening is active. Inspect authentication, route classification, private cache descriptors, connection policy, and storage backends for changes crossing trust boundaries.

Tests and CI were inspected for this brief, not executed. Existing tests are coverage signals, not passing results. When execution is authorized, use affected Rust tests plus relevant CLI suite modules; the smoke profile is only a broad sanity check. Rebuild the TypeScript CLI bundle before e2e testing. Report actual selected tests and results. Update affected documentation and release notes when required, using pacquet for Rust CLI changesets and pnpm for TypeScript CLI changesets. Keep edits focused, substantiate risks with exact source, and do not commit, push, publish, or access credentials without authorization.

system_map.summary: The repository has two CLI implementations and a sibling registry server, with shared Rust crates rather than one uniform runtime. The Rust CLI separates startup, command routing, application state, and the installation engine. pnpr builds an Axum server around configuration, identity, routing, storage, and optional protocol surfaces. Root manifests coordinate builds and tests across both language stacks.

claims.claim: The root Cargo workspace includes pnpm crates, pnpm task binaries, and pnpr crates; its shared package metadata selects Rust edition 2024.
The Rust executable's main delegates to pnpm_cli::main, which installs diagnostics and runs CLI startup on a separate thread; normal commands use a Tokio runtime with 32 MiB stack headroom.

The TypeScript entrypoint dynamically loads main and the worker API, routes errors through errorHandler, and drains workers in finally; its package ships bin launchers and dist output and requires Node >=22.13.
CLI State owns manifest data, a lazy wanted lockfile, resolved-package state, and shared HTTP/tarball caches; configuration is borrowed as a process-lifetime Config.

pnpr exposes library router/serve APIs and a Tokio binary; serve validates enabled surfaces and registry routing, loads OSV and authentication, builds the router, then binds and serves with graceful shutdown.

pnpr separates durable hosted storage from its disposable local proxy cache. HostedBackend supports local or S3-compatible implementations, while authentication supports local htpasswd/SQLite and selectable shared SQL backends.

Root scripts provide Rust build, affected tests, smoke tests, checks, and linting, alongside TypeScript compilation and package testing; pnpm-workspace.yaml wraps CI scripts in named pipelines and assigns task concurrency groups.

The Rust CLI's npm wrapper is named pacquet in-repo but publishes as pnpm and exposes pnpm/pn/pnpx/pnx. A separate workflow builds the pnpm container image for amd64 and arm64 with provenance and SBOM output.

feature_catalog.summary: The inspected Rust command table covers dependency management, workspace execution, package inspection, publishing, configuration, runtime management, and release intents. Installation exposes dependency-group and linker choices, with optional Cargo and Python participation. pnpr combines compatible registry APIs with resolution, artifact, compiler-cache, and pipeline-record surfaces. This catalog groups the inspected public surfaces; command registration alone does not establish complete implementation or successful operation.

claims.claim: Dependency commands include add, install, install-test, update, remove, link/unlink, import, dedupe, prune, fetch, deploy, and patch/patch-commit/patch-remove; install accepts production, development, and optional dependency selection plus isolated, hoisted, or PnP linkers.

Execution surfaces include recursive, run, exec, dlx, create, test/start/stop/restart shortcuts, tasks, and pipeline. Pipeline's declared contract includes frozen installation, affected-project selection, dependency ordering, and cached task restoration.
Inspection and security commands include list/ll, why, outdated, audit, peers, licenses, sbom, doctor, ignored-builds, approve-builds, cat-file, cat-index, and find-hash.

Publishing and account commands include pack, publish, stage, access, deprecate/undeprecate, unpublish, dist-tag, login/logout, owner, team, whoami, and star/unstar/stars; change, version, and lane manage release intents and lanes.

Configuration and environment surfaces include config/get/set, pkg, set-script, runtime, deprecated env, shim, with, setup, self-update, completion, clean/purge, ci, store, and cache. edit/profile/token/xmas are explicitly registered as unimplemented commands directing users to npm.

When cargo.enabled or python.enabled is set, ecosystem_install::plan adds Cargo or Python tasks to an InstallPlan; Python selection follows workspace scope and production/development dependency groups.

pnpr mounts npm metadata, version, tarball, search, dist-tag, publish, unpublish, and staged-publish routes, including named registry prefixes; configured Cargo and PyPI ecosystems add their own route sets.

Optional pnpr surfaces provide resolve/verify-lockfile, artifact publication/resolution/blob retrieval, compiler-cache reads and writes, and pipeline-run storage plus a viewer. NAPI separately exposes install, rebuild, pack, dependency resolution, peer checks, configuration, and lockfile APIs to Node hosts.

data_flow.summary: CLI inputs become normalized arguments, configuration, manifest data, and lazily loaded lockfile state before entering the installation engine. The engine carries explicit workspace scope, lockfile policy, execution mode, shared caches, and verification state through resolution and materialization. Installed metadata and freshness records represent different stages of completion. Server reads add identity and declared provenance before consulting hosted storage or upstream caches.

claims.claim: Rust startup consumes args_os, handles executable aliases and the pm prefix, extracts ConfigOverrides, rewrites with current, parses Clap arguments, and retains child argv for pinned-package-manager dispatch.
Config is a merged runtime type rather than directly deserialized file data: defaults are overlaid with the auth/registry/network subset of .npmrc and structural pnpm-workspace.yaml settings.

State::install passes shared tarball and HTTP caches, resolved packages, Config, PackageManifest, and a lazy lockfile into Install::new; dedicated-project installs also share cross-project caches and completion coordination.

InstallArgs converts CLI/config decisions into lockfile policy, execution mode, linker, architecture, and resolution seed settings. pnpr's remote policy controls server resolution, while local materialization uses the server-produced lockfile as frozen input.

RunExecution loads lockfiles and hooked manifests, settles the wanted lockfile, creates Verification, dispatches the chosen path, materializes, and applies the result; shared Verification holds metadata cache, planned canonical fetches, and resolution verifiers.

Installed-state commit builds and writes .modules.yaml, then saves the current lockfile. Workspace freshness is written later, and a moved-tree filtered install deliberately skips that freshness update.

pnpr metadata reads validate CanonicalPackageName, resolve a RegistrySource, authorize upstream access or apply hosted gates, then load bytes. Upstream responses pass through packument_response with tarball-base rewriting, OSV data, and abbreviated-response selection.

pnpr's resolution cache distinguishes public and private fetch routes using RouteClass and a Footprint digest. RouteHook selects server-managed credentials at the auth-selection boundary; privacy depends on registry/package policy rather than simply whether a request carried credentials.

behavior_traces.summary: Three principal flows were followed through source: CLI startup, dependency installation through installed-state persistence, and pnpr metadata/tarball reads through authorization and cache handling. Additional startup reading distinguishes pnpr's production server API from convenience router construction. The traces retain early returns and policy branches because those determine which work actually occurs. These are execution paths inferred directly from code structure, not observed runs.

claims.claim: Rust startup follows bin::main → pnpm_cli::main → run_on_big_stack(run_cli) → shim dispatch → argument normalization → parse_or_answer → configure_cli_args → pinned dispatch/completion checks → Rayon setup → install fast-path check → run_cli_command.

TypeScript startup follows buildArgv → runPnpm → main → parseCliArgs → loadCommandConfig/readCommandConfig → package-manager/runtime handling → config-dependency and hook loading → runCommandWithConfig; runPnpm finally drains workers.

InstallArgs::run calls run_inner, resolves frozen/link options, rejects pnpr plus dry-run, and selects install_via_pnpr_inner when pnpr_target exists; otherwise run_local builds State::install and invokes run or run_selected.

Local Install::run → run_inner acquires a store-use lock → run_inner_impl settles RunMode and discovers the workspace → RunExecution::run checks reuse, loads lockfiles, and settles wanted state → dispatch chooses frozen/fresh → materialize → finish_materialization.

Persistence follows finish_materialization → apply_materialization_result → apply → link_apply_projects → commit_apply_state → finish_apply. commit_modules_state writes module metadata before the current lockfile; finish_apply subsequently publishes workspace freshness and completion output.

pnpr startup follows Args::parse → Config::resolve_with_overrides → apply_cli_overrides → logging → serve. serve validates configuration, loads active OSV, calls load_startup_auth with registry journal recovery, builds routes, binds the listener, and enters graceful serving.

A metadata read follows serve_packument → addressed_registry → serve_registry_packument → canonical-name parsing/source selection/access authorization → serve_packument_via_upstream → load_upstream_packument. A fresh cache hit returns immediately; misses fetch and cache, authoritative 404s purge cached package state, and packument_response shapes the client response.

An upstream tarball read follows serve_registry_tarball → access authorization → serve_tarball_via_upstream → filename validation/authorized_upstream → serve_authorized_upstream_tarball. Without OSV, a cache hit can precede metadata binding; misses bind version/integrity, screen OSV, fetch, open temporary storage, and stream with integrity-gated cache promotion.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI definitions were inspected, not executed; no passing result, measured coverage percentage, or benchmark outcome is established here. Rust uses ordinary and Tokio tests, process-level CLI fixtures, snapshots, and cargo-nextest configuration. TypeScript uses Jest with registry-backed project fixtures. The inspected checks span installation, filtering, integrity, recovery, and language/runtime boundaries, but the bounded sample cannot establish all untested behavior.

claims.claim: The inspected Rust CLI suite is assembled in tests/suite/main.rs as one integration-test binary, while nextest runs individual tests in separate processes; its modules include install-related commands, custom resolvers/fetchers, lifecycle behavior, and linker variants.

should_install_dependencies spawns the real CLI against a mocked registry, asserts the direct dependency is a symlink/junction, checks transitive placement in the virtual store, and snapshots workspace/store structure using insta.

TypeScript install/only.ts uses Jest and execPnpm fixtures to check production/development filtering; its production test also checks progress counts and verifies the resolved dev-transitive version in the lockfile before store-presence assertions.

pnpr tarball tests use Tokio, mockito, temporary storage, and Axum oneshot requests to check declaring-version integrity binding and cache replay after router reconstruction; the same file includes a tampered-stream rejection test.

Journal-recovery tests fabricate interrupted on-disk publication state, including an older manifest format, to exercise sealed roll-forward and unsealed rollback; these recovery scenarios were read, not run.

The nextest smoke profile selects one test per behavior area and explicitly does not prove change correctness. Default tests receive a 60-second slow interval with termination after five intervals, and separate validation is documented for stale smoke-test names.

Rust CI invokes separate rust-test and pnpr-test pipelines and adds a Linux Node test of the built NAPI addon. TypeScript CI builds the bundle before sharded tests across Node 22.13, 24, and 26.10 on Linux, with a separate Windows shard matrix.

Ecosystem E2E and Cargo equivalence are scheduled compatibility checks rather than per-PR merge blockers; docs CI builds the external website with repository docs and checks URLs, while the inspected CodeQL matrix selects JavaScript.

risk_map.summary: The observations below identify trust boundaries and behavior that deserves careful review; they are not confirmed vulnerabilities. Package scripts and JavaScript hooks intentionally cross into process execution, while pnpr handles identity, remote fetches, cached private data, and persistent publication state. Several protections are explicit, including early authorization, integrity-gated cache promotion, connection policy, and verification gates. Operational assumptions and coverage limits remain relevant even when those protections are present.

claims.claim: The executor exposes shell execution through sh -c and allows callers to choose the working directory; command strings therefore cross an intentional code-execution boundary, and nonzero child status is distinct from spawn/wait errors.

pnpmfile hooks execute JavaScript in Node processes. readPackage/afterAllResolved/filterLog use a lazy long-lived worker, while preResolution uses node -e with piped JSON and a 30-second timeout; preResolution failures warn rather than abort.

Lockfile verification can overlap resolution/fetching but must gate sensitive downstream operations. The gate aborts on drop; trustLockfile or an empty verifier set makes verification a no-op, so changes to either policy or completion ordering require review.

pnpr mounts authentication before handlers to enforce token restrictions before buffering large write bodies. Unknown or revoked ordinary bearer tokens can resolve to anonymous, leaving route and per-package policy responsible for distinguishing public access from protected operations.

Resolver connection policy admits public addresses, explicitly allowed private networks, and the server's configured public_url host. IP literals are checked separately from hostname resolution; own-host configuration and private-network exceptions are security-sensitive inputs.

A warm upstream tarball cache hit without OSV intentionally skips re-binding against current metadata, so previously verified bytes can remain downloadable after a version is unpublished. The documented acceptance authority is the client's lockfile integrity.

Inference: install completion is a broad regression hotspot because filtered selection, prior metadata, current lockfiles, and workspace freshness meet at separate writes; reordering freshness ahead of module/current-lockfile commit could advertise an incomplete tree.

The inspected CodeQL workflow selects only JavaScript, and the smoke profile explicitly limits its correctness claim. Neither source establishes Rust security-analysis coverage or full branch coverage; broader repository tooling was not exhaustively audited.

extension_points.summary: The clearest extension seams are typed command registration, ordered resolver composition, hook interfaces, reporter events, and backend traits. pnpr separates feature-surface mounting from registry provenance and storage implementation. Extension contracts frequently encode security or compatibility constraints, so adding an implementation requires preserving those constraints rather than only satisfying a type signature. NAPI exposes a separate host-facing boundary over the same Rust engine.

claims.claim: CliCommand is a Clap-derived enum carrying command-specific argument types, with aliases and an external-subcommand fallback; cli_args::grammar caches the assembled command grammar in OnceLock.

DefaultResolver composes Vec<Box<dyn Resolver>> in order: Ok(None) defers, the first claim wins, and exhaustion yields a stable unsupported-spec error; resolving-resolver-base also exposes a separate ResolutionVerifier seam.

PnpmfileHooks is an async Send+Sync interface for manifest and resolution customization. Custom fetchers can request native CafsInfo, TempDir, LocalTarball, and RemoteTarball operations through callback channels with oneshot responses.

Reporter extensions add typed LogEvent variants serialized with a name tag; channel names and payloads are designed for consumption by the TypeScript default reporter, making the wire contract part of extension correctness.

pnpr surface_routes conditionally mounts resolver, artifact, pipeline, and registry route factories. Shared authentication/body-limit layering is applied after surface construction, and individual protocol routes add caller gates.

Registry supports Hosted, Upstream, and ordered Router variants with declared package patterns. A router selects a claiming concrete source authoritatively; its not-found/unavailable result cannot fall through to a different origin.

Storage and identity implementations plug into HostedBackend and AuthState's UserBackend/TokenBackend trait objects. Hosted backends own compare-and-set and blob-promotion differences; backend selection occurs during startup.

The NAPI crate exports typed install, resolution, configuration, packing, and lockfile boundaries; its documented JS contract lives in the wrapper declarations, and module initialization installs the engine's tracing subscriber.

claims.claim: Read AGENTS.md and PHILOSOPHY.md plus the owning product's guide. New CLI features belong only in Rust v12; shared bugs require fixes in both supported implementations, while pnpr has no CLI counterpart to mirror.
Prefer existing capabilities and shared abstractions before adding code. pnpr specifically directs reuse of pnpm crates and reserves pnpr-prefixed crates for registry-only logic.

Run Rust tooling from the repository root and account for pnpm-managed Cargo source replacement. A fresh clone or changed Cargo.lock requires dependency installation before Cargo can resolve the replaced sources; cargo add is not the documented dependency-addition path.

For authorized Rust validation, use pnpm test:rust-affected and add relevant pnpm-cli suite modules for user-visible engine changes: affected-crate selection alone does not necessarily include CLI e2e tests. Invoke root pnpm scripts to participate in task concurrency limits.

Tests and CI in this brief were inspected, not executed. A future agent must establish actual selected-test results; smoke is explicitly insufficient to prove correctness, and TypeScript CLI e2e tests require rebuilding the bundled dist/pnpm.mjs after package changes.

For pnpr embedding, choose APIs deliberately: router uses in-memory auth, router_with_auth can panic on invalid setup, and try_router variants return errors. Production serve loads persistent auth and recovers registry publication state before binding.

User-visible changes require affected-version documentation and normally a changeset, with an exemption for bugs in unreleased features. Target pacquet for Rust CLI changes, pnpm plus affected packages for TypeScript fixes, and @pnpm/pnpr for server changes.

Preserve reporter event payload/order for shared fixes and use real temporary-directory or mocked-registry fixtures before introducing test injection. Root README still calls the Rust port experimental, while product docs identify v12 as the development target; verify maturity from current policy and feature evidence.
